hints: Start by linking location to function - mitochondria supply energy locally, so list which processes in a neurone ending and in a muscle fibre need a constant energy supply.
In the presynaptic knob, think about how the transmitter acetylcholine is made and how vesicles get to the membrane and release their contents.
In the sarcomere, think about the sliding filament cycle - what has to be moved against a concentration gradient for relaxation to happen.
Also in the sarcomere, think about what ATP binding to myosin allows - detachment of the cross-bridge and resetting the myosin head for the next power stroke.
walkthrough:
Why many mitochondria means high ATP demand**
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to make ATP. Where you see clusters of mitochondria, a lot of ATP is used very quickly and needs to be made on the spot. So split your answer into two places: the presynaptic knob and the sarcomere.

Presynaptic knob - paying for transmitter release**
When an action potential arrives, synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release acetylcholine by exocytosis. Making acetylcholine and moving vesicles to the membrane and fusing them all need ATP. That is why the knob is packed with mitochondria.

Sarcomere - paying for contraction and relaxation**
In striated muscle, ATP is needed to keep cycling cross-bridges. ATP binding detaches the myosin head from actin and lets it cock back to its starting position. ATP is also needed to actively pump $Ca^{2+}$ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using $Ca^{2+}$ ATPase, which lowers sarcoplasmic $Ca^{2+}$ and allows relaxation.

Final answer: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration. In presynaptic knob: ATP for synthesis of acetylcholine and for movement / exocytosis of vesicles. In sarcomere: ATP for active transport of $Ca^{2+}$ into sarcoplasmic reticulum and for detachment of myosin heads / breaking cross-bridges and resetting myosin.

hints: Remember the trigger for an action potential - the postsynaptic membrane must be depolarised to threshold, so focus on whether the membrane becomes less negative or more negative.
Compare the charge effect: entry of positive $Na^{+}$ versus entry of negative $Cl^{-}$ on the inside of the membrane.
For stimulation together, think about summation - what is the net change in charge when depolarisation and hyperpolarisation happen at the same time.
walkthrough:
X alone - excitatory effect**
Acetylcholine from X opens $Na^{+}$ channels. $Na^{+}$ rushes in, making the inside less negative. That is depolarisation. If threshold is reached, voltage-gated channels open and an action potential fires. So statement 1 is correct - agree.

Y alone - inhibitory effect**
Glutamate from Y in this example opens $Cl^{-}$ channels. $Cl^{-}$ rushes in, making the inside more negative. That is hyperpolarisation. The membrane moves away from threshold, so no action potential can start. There is also no $Na^{+}$ influx to depolarise. So statement 2 is wrong - disagree.

X and Y together - cancellation**
When both fire together, you get spatial summation of opposite effects. The positive charge entering as $Na^{+}$ is balanced by negative charge entering as $Cl^{-}$. Net membrane potential stays near resting and does not reach threshold. So no action potential occurs. Statement 3 is correct - agree.

Final answer: 1. Agree - $Na^{+}$ influx causes depolarisation to threshold so action potential occurs. 2. Disagree - $Cl^{-}$ influx causes hyperpolarisation / no $Na^{+}$ influx so no depolarisation, so no action potential. 3. Agree - $Na^{+}$ influx is cancelled / balanced by $Cl^{-}$ influx so threshold not reached, so no action potential.

hints: Start from the normal job of myelin - an electrical insulator that forces action potentials to jump between nodes.
Think about what is left when that insulation is lost - where can local circuits form and how does that change speed.
walkthrough:
What myelin normally does**
Myelin insulates the axon so $Na^{+}$ and $K^{+}$ cannot move across the myelinated regions. Depolarisation at one node of Ranvier sets up long local circuits to the next node, so the action potential appears to jump - saltatory conduction, which is very fast and saves energy.

Effect of breakdown**
If myelin breaks down, insulation is lost. Charge leaks out and only short local circuits can form. Saltatory conduction is lost or reduced, so action potentials must be regenerated continuously along the whole membrane. That is much slower and may even fail.
Final answer: Speed of transmission decreases. Loss of saltatory conduction so impulse must be regenerated continuously along axon / only short local circuits form.
